title: The single life
hook: single people also live a calling of love and service

segments.voice: Yesterday, marriage as calling: the couple giving the sacrament to each other, and Paul's great sacrament. Your line was holy through each other.

A question single people sometimes get at family weddings: so, when's it your turn? Asked kindly, over cake, as if life were a waiting room and the real thing starts at the altar. Meanwhile, look at one single man's week. Tuesday, he drives his elderly neighbor to the cardiologist. Wednesday, he's the one his sister calls at midnight. Saturday, he coaches nine-year-olds who think he's the funniest man alive. Sunday, he reads at the early Mass. Nobody at the wedding asked about any of that.
screen: `WHEN'S IT YOUR TURN?` → `A WEEK OF ONE SINGLE MAN.` → `NOBODY ASKED ABOUT THAT.`

segments.voice: Start with something easy to skip: the Gospels give Jesus no wife. Neither, as far as his letters let us see, did Paul, and he writes about it to Corinth with real warmth. In the Douay-Rheims: "For I would that all men were even as myself: but every one hath his proper gift from God; one after this manner, and another after that." Notice the word gift. Marriage is a gift; so is the unmarried life. Then he says why it matters: "He that is without a wife, is solicitous for the things that belong to the Lord, how he may please God." The unmarried person, Paul says, has room: for prayer, for friends, for people who need someone to show up. The Catechism speaks to single people directly. It says many live single not by their own choice, because of the circumstances of their lives, and that they are especially close to the heart of Jesus. It asks parishes to open their doors to them, and says no one is without a family in this world: the Church is a home and family for everyone. So the Catholic picture isn't of a person waiting for a vocation to begin. The call to holiness from two days ago is already theirs, whole. Some single people take a vow later, some marry later, and some live single all their lives. None of those seasons is a gap in the calling. Love and service don't need a ring to count. The neighbor at the cardiologist knows that.
screen: `THE GOSPELS GIVE JESUS NO WIFE.` · `EVERY ONE HATH HIS PROPER GIFT.` · `ROOM FOR THE THINGS OF THE LORD.` · `THE CHURCH IS A HOME FOR EVERYONE.` · then, large: `EVERY ONE HATH HIS PROPER GIFT FROM GOD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you know who is single, a friend, an aunt, a widower down the street, or yourself, and one specific way they show up for people: the drive, the call, the meal. If you pray, thank God for them by name, and ask that they be loved as they love. If you don't, let gratitude for them fill the sit.
The single life. In Catholic teaching, a life lived unmarried, by choice or by circumstance, that is already a whole calling to love and service. Today's word.
Your line: a whole calling. No season of life is a waiting room. Day one thousand four hundred eight.

howItsDone: Single Catholics live the call to holiness in their work, friendships, family and parish, without vows of religious life. The Catechism asks parishes to welcome single people and describes the Church as a home and family for everyone.

chat.says: I never married. Does the Church think I missed my vocation?
options: No. Catholic teaching says the call to holiness is already yours, whole; single life isn't a gap.
Yes. The Church teaches that holiness is only for people who marry or take vows.
It depends on age: after forty, the Church counts single life as a calling.
chat.meaning: The Catechism says single people are especially close to Jesus's heart, and the call to holiness is already theirs; love and service need no ring.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of 1 Corinthians 7:7 and 7:32: confirm exactly.
'Neither, as far as his letters let us see, did Paul' leans on 1 Corinthians 7:7–8; some readers argue Paul was a widower. Phrased cautiously; confirm.

CCC 1658 (single persons, often not of their choosing, especially close to Jesus' heart; the doors of homes and parishes open to them; 'no one is without a family in this world') paraphrased; confirm. The Catechism says 'great number'; the script says 'many', which the text supports.
Greek ἄγαμος in 1 Corinthians 7:32: confirm spelling and pronunciation.
The hook's single man is an illustrative scene, not a real person.
